power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Midlife and older women living with HIV often carry several co-occurring social and behavioral stressors, and how that accumulated burden relates to cardiovascular risk is not well described.

We examined whether cumulative syndemic burden was associated with estimated 10-year risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease among women aged 45 years and older, and whether menopause stage modified it.
Data came from the MACS/WIHS Combined Cohort Study, a multisite United States cohort, for visits between October 2020 and March 2025.
The full sample included 1,993 women, 1,446 of them living with HIV; a secondary sample of 1,063 women virally suppressed at baseline contributed 4,009 visits.
Syndemic burden was the sum of six conditions: elevated depressive symptoms, current tobacco use, hazardous alcohol use, recent stimulant use, physical inactivity, and material insecurity.

Ten-year cardiovascular risk was estimated with the Pooled Cohort Equations and modeled with linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts; random forest classifiers were trained separately to predict high estimated risk (7.5 percent or greater).
Median age was 56 years, 63 percent were non-Hispanic Black, and 57 percent reported two or more syndemic conditions.

Each additional syndemic condition was associated with a 0.40-point higher estimated risk score (95 percent confidence interval 0.01 to 0.78; p=0.043), and postmenopausal status with a 1.3-point higher score than premenopause (0.39 to 2.3; p=0.006).
The syndemic burden by menopause stage interaction was not significant overall (p=0.2), although an exploratory signal was present among virally suppressed women (0.50; p=0.079).

The classifiers discriminated moderately (areas under the curve 0.727 and 0.704); serum creatinine, body mass index, syndemic burden, and postmenopausal status ranked among the most important predictors.

Syndemic burden and reproductive aging were each independently and modestly associated with higher estimated cardiovascular risk, supporting joint assessment of both in risk stratification for midlife women with and without HIV.
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death among women in the United States and remains a dominant driver of morbidity across the life course [1].
text.formatted: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death among women in the United States and remains a dominant driver of morbidity across the life course <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Among people living with HIV (PLWH), improved survival with contemporary antiretroviral therapy has shifted clinical priorities toward chronic comorbidities, including CVD [2].
text.formatted: Among people living with HIV (PLWH), improved survival with contemporary antiretroviral therapy has shifted clinical priorities toward chronic comorbidities, including CVD <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: An American Heart Association scientific statement emphasizes that CVD risk in PLWH reflects the combined influence of traditional cardiometabolic risk factors and HIV-related mechanisms, including persistent immune activation and systemic inflammation [3].
text.formatted: An American Heart Association scientific statement emphasizes that CVD risk in PLWH reflects the combined influence of traditional cardiometabolic risk factors and HIV-related mechanisms, including persistent immune activation and systemic inflammation <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Among women living with HIV (WLWH), cardiovascular vulnerability is multifactorial, involving intersecting pathways linking traditional risk factors, metabolic dysregulation, reproductive aging, and chronic immune activation [4].
text.formatted: Among women living with HIV (WLWH), cardiovascular vulnerability is multifactorial, involving intersecting pathways linking traditional risk factors, metabolic dysregulation, reproductive aging, and chronic immune activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Studying this vulnerability requires analytic strategies that incorporate reproductive aging stage and contextual risk domains alongside traditional clinical factors.
Syndemic theory provides a framework for integrating these contextual drivers.
Syndemics describe the clustering of multiple adverse conditions within harmful social contexts, producing excess disease burden beyond what any single condition would predict [5].
text.formatted: Syndemics describe the clustering of multiple adverse conditions within harmful social contexts, producing excess disease burden beyond what any single condition would predict <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: In HIV research, syndemic frameworks conceptualize how co-occurring psychosocial and behavioral conditions concentrate in marginalized populations and jointly shape health vulnerability [6].
text.formatted: In HIV research, syndemic frameworks conceptualize how co-occurring psychosocial and behavioral conditions concentrate in marginalized populations and jointly shape health vulnerability <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Empirically, syndemic patterns involving unhealthy alcohol use, smoking, and depressive symptoms have been associated with increased incident CVD among people with and without HIV, supporting the relevance of cumulative burden to cardiovascular risk stratification [7].
text.formatted: Empirically, syndemic patterns involving unhealthy alcohol use, smoking, and depressive symptoms have been associated with increased incident CVD among people with and without HIV, supporting the relevance of cumulative burden to cardiovascular risk stratification <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Menopause represents a biologically distinct interval of reproductive aging during which endocrine remodeling intersects with cardiometabolic physiology.

Longitudinal and mechanistic evidence demonstrated that the menopause transition is associated with distinct patterns of change in endogenous sex hormones and adverse shifts in body fat distribution, lipids and lipoproteins, and vascular health, processes that are plausibly relevant for subsequent ASCVD risk and prevention timing [8].
text.formatted: Longitudinal and mechanistic evidence demonstrated that the menopause transition is associated with distinct patterns of change in endogenous sex hormones and adverse shifts in body fat distribution, lipids and lipoproteins, and vascular health, processes that are plausibly relevant for subsequent ASCVD risk and prevention timing <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Standard cardiovascular risk prediction tools -including the ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) [9] -have demonstrated systematic underestimation of observed CVD risk in HIV cohorts, with calibration problems particularly pronounced in women [10, 11].
text.formatted: Standard cardiovascular risk prediction tools -including the ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> -have demonstrated systematic underestimation of observed CVD risk in HIV cohorts, with calibration problems particularly pronounced in women <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">11]</ref>.

text.text: PCE does not incorporate psychosocial and structural determinants of cardiovascular health, including material insecurity, depression, and substance use, which are especially prevalent among WLWH and may independently drive cardiometabolic risk trajectories [12] [13] [14] [15] [16].
text.formatted: PCE does not incorporate psychosocial and structural determinants of cardiovascular health, including material insecurity, depression, and substance use, which are especially prevalent among WLWH and may independently drive cardiometabolic risk trajectories <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[16]</ref>.

text.text: Despite this rationale, much prior CVD research in HIV has emphasized isolated risk factors rather than cumulative burden of co-occurring vulnerabilities.

This leaves a gap in the literature for WLWH, for whom depression, tobacco and substance use, physical inactivity, and material hardship may cluster within individuals and potentially amplify cardiovascular vulnerability through behavioral and psychosocial mechanisms.

A syndemic approach is therefore well suited to characterize how multiple co-occurring conditions relate to cardiovascular risk profiles and cardiovascular morbidity in WLWH, while recognizing that such measures may reflect broader vulnerability rather than a direct causal mechanism.

Using longitudinal data from the MACS/WIHS Combined Cohort Study, a large observational cohort designed to understand chronic comorbidities among PLWH and comparable without HIV participants [17], this study evaluates syndemic burden and menopause stage as primary exposures in relation to estimated 10-year ASCVD risk (continuous and dichotomous at ≥7.5%), and uses random forest classifiers to characterize important predictors of high ASCVD risk in a population with intersecting biological and psychosocial risk domains.

text.text: This study is a secondary analysis of de-identified data from the MACS/WIHS Combined Cohort Study (MWCCS).
The MWCCS protocol was approved by the institutional review board at each participating site, all participants provided written informed consent, and the study followed the Declaration of Helsinki.
The present analysis was conducted under an approved MWCCS data analysis request.
Data were accessed for research purposes on 20 October 2025, and the authors did not have access to information that could identify individual participants during or after data collection.

MWCCS is a prospective observational cohort in the United States designed to study chronic health conditions affecting PLWH and comparable participants without HIV, integrating legacy cohorts and harmonized follow-up.
Details have been previously described [17].
text.formatted: Details have been previously described <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[17]</ref>.

text.text: For the present longitudinal analysis, baseline and follow-up data were obtained through MWCCS visit windows spanning V101 (Oct 1, 2020-Sep 30, 2021), V102 (Oct 1, 2021-Sep 30, 2022), V103 (Oct 1, 2022-Sep 30, 2023), V104 (Oct 1, 2023-Sep 30, 2024), and V1051 (Oct 1, 2024-Mar 31, 2025).

Participants living with or without HIV were eligible for the full analytic cohort if they were women enrolled in MWCCS, were aged ≥45 years, and contributed at least two study visits during V101-V1051.
Participant flow and analytic sample construction are summarized in Fig 1.

text.text: Two analytic populations were prespecified.
The primary population was the full analytic sample comprising 1,993 women, including 1,446 women living with HIV (WLWH) and 547 women without HIV (Fig 1).
text.formatted: The primary population was the full analytic sample comprising 1,993 women, including 1,446 women living with HIV (WLWH) and 547 women without HIV (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The secondary analytic population was restricted to WLWH who were virally suppressed at baseline (HIV RNA <50 copies/mL), yielding 1,063 participants; 383 WLWH were excluded from this sub-sample because they were not suppressed at baseline or had missing baseline viral load.

text.text: The suppressed WLWH sub-sample contributed 4,009 total visits across follow-up.
MACS/WIHS Combined Cohort Study (MWCCS).
Women aged 45 years or older seen between October 2020 and March 2025 were eligible.
The full analytic sample comprised 1,993 women (1,446 women living with HIV [WLWH]; 547 women without HIV).
The virally suppressed subcohort included 1,063 WLWH contributing 4,009 person-visits.
The primary continuous cardiovascular outcome was the 10-year ASCVD risk score, modeled longitudinally as a continuous measure.

ASCVD risk estimation followed the ACC/AHA pooled cohort equations (PCE) framework [9], which uses age, race, lipids, blood pressure and treatment, diabetes status, and smoking status to estimate 10-year ASCVD risk.
text.formatted: ASCVD risk estimation followed the ACC/AHA pooled cohort equations (PCE) framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>, which uses age, race, lipids, blood pressure and treatment, diabetes status, and smoking status to estimate 10-year ASCVD risk.

text.text: A binary highrisk outcome was also defined as 10-year ASCVD risk ≥7.5%, reflecting a commonly used guideline-relevant threshold for risk stratification and preventive therapy discussions.

Syndemic burden was operationalized as a cumulative syndemic score ranging from 0 to 6, derived from six binary conditions defined in the analytic dataset: elevated depressive symptoms, current tobacco use, hazardous alcohol use, recent stimulant use, physical inactivity, and material insecurity.
For descriptive analyses, syndemic burden was also categorized as 0 conditions, 1 condition, and ≥2 conditions.

Menopause stage was modeled as a categorical exposure aligned with reproductive aging staging principles and the STRAW+10 framework, operationalized as premenopause, perimenopause, and postmenopause (natural and/or surgical).
Models adjusted for sociodemographic and clinical covariates including education, employment, insurance, BMI, hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia.
HIV-related factors were incorporated when appropriate.
Age and race/ethnicity were excluded from ASCVD risk models to avoid circular adjustment, as these variables are embedded in the PCE.

The random forest models used 32 predictors spanning behavioral/syndemic factors, clinical comorbidities, biomarkers, psychosocial variables, and cognitive indicators, with PCE-embedded variables intentionally excluded to avoid tautological prediction.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize baseline demographic, clinical, and behavioral characteristics of the participants, stratified by the HIV status and syndemic factors among WLWH, and also for syndemic factors among virally suppressed WLWH subsample.

Particularly, we used median (Q1, Q3) for continuous variables and n (%) for categorical variables, with group comparisons using Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum tests for continuous variables and Fisher's exact tests for categorical variables.
Linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts assessed longitudinal associations with continuous ASCVD risk.
Random slopes were not included given convergence considerations.
Models included time, syndemic score, menopause stage, and their interaction.
HIV status was a fixed effect in the full sample and omitted by design in the suppressed sub-sample.

Complementing the mixed-effects regression approach, random forest classifiers were used to predict high ASCVD risk (≥7.5%), without pre-specifying functional form or interaction terms, thereby capturing potential nonlinear relationships and complex interactions among predictors.
Random forests are ensemble tree methods that aggregate predictions across many decorrelated decision trees to reduce variance and improve generalization.

Model development followed a participant-level train-test workflow, such that all visits from a given participant were assigned to either the training set or the held-out test set to avoid within-person leakage.
The training/test split, stratified by outcome, was 70/30 for the full analytic sample and 60/40 for the virally suppressed sub-cohort.

With the number of trees fixed at 1,000, hyperparameters (number of predictors sampled at each split and minimum node size) were tuned using 5-fold crossvalidation on the training set, and performance was evaluated on the held-out test set using AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV.
Variable importance was assessed using impurity-based (Gini) importance; these rankings are descriptive and should not be interpreted as causal estimates.
Models were developed separately for the full analytic sample and the virally suppressed sub-cohort.
Reporting followed TRIPOD recommendations for clinical prediction models [18].
text.formatted: Reporting followed TRIPOD recommendations for clinical prediction models <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Missing data were addressed using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; m=5 imputations, maxit=5 iterations), with logistic regression for binary variables, predictive mean matching for continuous variables, and polytomous regression for nominal variables.
All analyses were performed in R (version 4.5.2).

In this longitudinal analysis of midlife and older women in the MWCCS, higher syndemic burden and postmenopausal status were each independently associated with higher estimated ASCVD risk in the full analytic sample.

Each additional syndemic condition was associated with a statistically significant but modest increase in continuous estimated ASCVD risk, and postmenopausal status was associated with higher estimated ASCVD risk compared with premenopause.
The syndemic-by-menopause interaction was not statistically significant overall, though an exploratory signal was observed among virally suppressed WLWH.
Random forest classifiers ranked syndemic score, BMI, serum creatinine, and postmenopausal status among the consistent top predictors of high estimated ASCVD risk across both analytic populations.

Machine learning approaches complement traditional regression by capturing potential nonlinear relationships and providing hypothesis-generating variable prioritization for future risk prediction tool development.
Importantly, menopause is associated with a narrowing of the traditional sex-based protection against cardiovascular disease.

As endogenous estrogen declines during the menopausal transition, estrogen-mediated vasodilatory and anti-inflammatory effects are attenuated, and women's cardiovascular risk profiles converge toward those of age-matched men.

This phenomenon is clinically relevant because it situates postmenopausal WLWH -who face both HIV-related immune activation and the hormonal shifts of menopause -at potentially heightened cardiovascular vulnerability. [19, 20, 21] The observed association between postmenopausal status and higher estimated ASCVD risk is biologically plausible: the menopause transition involves endocrine changes associated with adverse shifts in lipid profiles, body fat distribution, and vascular function -all upstream determinants of ASCVD risk [8, 19].

text.text: The consistent ranking of syndemic score among top predictors in both random forest models reinforces its value as a summary index of modifiable vulnerability.

Although the syndemic-by-postmenopause interaction was not significant in the full sample, the exploratory signal in the virally suppressed sub-cohort (p=0.079) suggests that postmenopausal WLWH with higher syndemic burden may warrant further evaluation.
Larger samples or longer follow-up are needed to evaluate this possible amplification effect.
These findings have clinical relevance in the context of updated cardiovascular prevention guidelines.
The 2026 AHA/ACC cholesterol management guidelines recommend LDL-lowering therapy for adults aged 40-75 years with HIV irrespective of LDL-C level.

Our finding that syndemic burden was associated with higher estimated ASCVD risk, after accounting for HIV status and selected clinical and social covariates while avoiding circular adjustment for PCE-embedded variables, suggests that syndemic screening may help identify WLWH who could benefit from intensified cardiovascular prevention efforts. text.text: The analytic approach combined mixed-effects inference and prediction modeling, explicitly addressing circularity concerns by excluding PCE components from machine learning predictors.
Several limitations require consideration.

First, ASCVD risk was a computed estimator rather than an observed event outcome, and PCE-based risk estimation has recognized limitations in HIV populations, including evidence of underestimation and sex differences in calibration; associations with the risk score should not be interpreted as direct evidence of proportional changes in adjudicated event incidence [10].

text.text: Because the PCE incorporates age, the estimated time effect partly reflects aging embedded in the risk equation as well as changes in measured risk factors over follow-up.

Second, the PREVENT equation [24] -a more contemporary risk tool that incorporates kidney function and a social deprivation index -was available from the DACC at the V1051 visit only, which did not support the full longitudinal analysis spanning V101 through V1051; future work should validate these findings using PREVENT once data become available across all visits.

Third, individual PCE components were intentionally excluded from the random forest predictor set; however, current tobacco use is included within the composite syndemic score, so the syndemic score is not fully independent of all PCE inputs.
Physical inactivity is not a PCE component but is correlated with cardiometabolic risk, and both features may influence random forest variable importance for estimated ASCVD risk models.

Because impurity-based Gini importance can favor continuous or high-cardinality predictors, variable-importance rankings should be interpreted as descriptive prioritization; future work should examine permutation importance and external validation.

Fourth, syndemic burden components were equally weighted (each scored 0/1); sensitivity analyses with differential weighting or latent class approaches were not performed and may yield different findings.

Additionally, because syndemic components were measured cross-sectionally at each visit, the temporal ordering of syndemic burden relative to changes in ASCVD risk cannot be established, and causal inference is not supported.

Fifth, menopause staging was based on self-reported menses and documented surgical history; menopause status was treated as a time-varying covariate updated at each study visit based on self-reported menses and documented surgical history; cases with apparent reversal from postmenopausal to perimenopausal staging were retained as reported and imputed using polytomous regression in the multiple imputation step.

Finally, non-adjudicated CVD events were not included as an outcome in this analysis, as MWCCS event adjudication is ongoing; associations between syndemic burden and incident cardiovascular events will be examined in future work once adjudicated data are available.
Among midlife and older women in the MWCCS, syndemic burden and postmenopausal status were each independently associated with higher longitudinal estimated ASCVD risk.

Random forest classifiers demonstrated moderate discrimination for high estimated ASCVD risk, with syndemic score, BMI, serum creatinine, and postmenopausal status consistently ranked among the top predictors.

These findings support integrating both reproductive aging stage and syndemic burden into cardiovascular risk assessment strategies for women aging with and without HIV, and support the need for syndemic-informed prevention approaches in this population.
